item.title: Katherine Clark launches majority leader bid
item.description: The Massachusetts Democrat currently serves as Hakeem Jeffries' No. 2.

media:content.media:title: House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) delivers remarks during a watch party at the AC Hotel Capitol Hill on Election Day in Washington, D.C. on Nov. 3, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts officially announced her bid for majority leader in a letter to colleagues Thursday.

Clark, currently the No. 2 to Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, is widely considered a shoo-in among her colleagues. She is currently unopposed, and if she wins, she would be the first woman with the title and most progressive member of the top leadership trio that is also expected to include Jeffries as speaker and Rep. Pete Aguilar as whip.

In line with leadership’s campaign message, Clark emphasized “Affordability, Affordability, Affordability” in her pitch to the caucus. Specifically, she named “ending the reckless war in Iran, rescinding Trump’s tariffs, reversing Republicans’ catastrophic cuts to healthcare and food assistance, curing off their giveaways to the Epstein Class, and pursuing rigorous oversight of this corrupt administration.”

To wrangle House Democrats’ massive majority — which is tracking to reach over 255 seats — Clark vowed to members: “At every decision point, I intend to work closely with you to understand the needs of your district and maximize your ability to deliver for your constituents.”

“Democrats will succeed by working as a team.” she added.

Clark will get a vote during House Democratic leadership elections scheduled for Nov. 18 and 19.

item.title: Trump loyalists face off to lead a decimated House GOP
item.description: Both Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise are close presidential allies, suggesting no clean break is imminent.

media:content.media:title: Scalise (right) has served in House GOP leadership for more than a decade, most recently under Speaker Mike Johnson (left).

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
House Republicans are responding to the resounding rebuke of their party by launching headlong into a leadership contest where neither candidate appears willing to break with the person congressional Republicans most blame for the sweeping midterm losses: President Donald Trump.

Both Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise are known to their colleagues as close Trump allies, and neither indicated they intend to put any daylight into their relationships with the president in their initial statements declaring their intention to run for minority leader.

Jordan, the longtime conservative brawler and sitting Judiciary chair, pledged to push back on Democratic excesses including “investigating every facet of the Administration and private entities across the country.”

Scalise, the current majority leader and a fixture of GOP leadership for more than a decade, also raised the prospect of pushing back against Democratic investigations and a possible Trump impeachment while telling colleagues that the president needed a “tested negotiator working alongside him to secure administration priorities.”

Those pledges to fight Democrats on Trump’s behalf came at the same time that other members were musing both publicly and privately about the president’s rapidly waning influence — and the imperative for lawmakers to start taking steps to craft a political future without him in it.

“Let’s start being a separate branch of government,” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), who is retiring at the end of the year, said in a text message about the election. “We’re not an appendage of the White House.”

Few House Republicans expect Scalise or Jordan to publicly break with Trump, which would be wildly out of character for either of them. Scalise traveled with the president during the final days of the midterm campaign season, and Jordan rose from a hard-right rabble-rouser to a cable-news fixture in part by embracing Trump.

Trump, for his part, said Wednesday he’s not planning to weigh in on the upcoming GOP leadership race that erupted immediately after Speaker Mike Johnson announced he would step aside as top House Republican in the next Congress.

“We’ll stay out of it,” Trump said. “All good people. I guess right now you have two candidates, right?”

Candidates in other House GOP leadership races similarly did not mention the need for the party to chart an independent course, but most stressed party unity and prioritizing members’ nuts-and-bolts concerns.

Members, meanwhile, spent Wednesday talking privately among themselves about the historic electoral wipeout — which could see Democrats win 260 seats, more than they’ve had since the early 1990s — and Trump’s role in bringing it about.

Trump responded to the loss by arguing Republicans simply do not vote if he is not on the ballot — cold comfort for lawmakers who will never appear on a ballot with Trump again.

A House Republican, one of several granted anonymity to speak candidly about the president and the upcoming leadership race, predicted many members would start creating distance from the president “quickly” upon their return to Washington as they come to terms with a post-Trump future.

“I’ve been totally wrong on that before,” the member added. But “I just don’t see how any amount of contorting can polish up this turd.”

Another GOP lawmaker lamented that Trump had not gotten more honest feedback from fellow Republicans sooner.

“They didn't call him out on things they didn't like, over fear of retribution,” the member said. “And that's a real problem.”

It’s an open question whether Jordan or Scalise would be equipped to do that. Jordan, a founder of the ultraconservative Freedom Caucus, pitched himself in a letter to colleagues as an expert in combating the hard-nosed investigations that Democrats are pledging to launch into Trump and other targets.

“I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats' playbook,” Jordan said in a letter to colleagues. “I know what it will take to lead our Conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats' tactics.”

Underscoring his support on the right, Jordan won an endorsement from the leader of the hard-line Club for Growth Wednesday. David McIntosh, a former House Republican, called Jordan “principled, politically savvy, [a] prolific fundraiser, and the best communicator” for the House GOP.

Scalise, whom many members see as the more moderate option, emphasized his past fundraising and legislative efforts and focused on the battle to regain the House majority — calling it his “number one goal as Republican leader.”

A third House Republican noted Scalise has to walk a fine line between being a known quantity and part of a leadership team that stayed tied to Trump’s hip.

“If people are looking for the steady hand, again, I think he's a guy to watch,” the member said. "But we got our asses kicked. And are they going to blame Scalise for that or the president? … Johnson already did, but does his first mate have to walk the plank, too?"

In his letter, Scalise called on House Republicans to “stand united as one team, be smart and strategic to secure conservative policy wins where we can, closely coordinate our defense against aggressive oversight and together develop a clear vision and agenda to earn back the majority in 2028.”

But as the prospect of having to turn 40 or more seats sunk in on Wednesday, Republicans took stock of whether the majority would be back in reach in two years.

A fourth GOP lawmaker said the goal of 2028 flip was not “realistic” and said Republicans were better-served to adopt a battle posture as Democrats threaten investigations and impeachments. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the likely incoming Oversight chair, told targets Tuesday night to “lawyer up.”

“Is there somebody better built for that than Jim Jordan?” the Republican said.

item.title: Capitol agenda: House GOP’s old guard is in for a fight
item.description: Party elections will test how closely GOP members — angry over Republicans’ deep defeats — tie their existing leadership team to the thrashing.

media:content.media:title: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise speaks during a Wednesday press conference at the U.S. Capitol on March 25, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy and Calen Razor
item.dc:contributor: By Mia McCarthy and Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
House Republican leadership races after the party’s catastrophic losses are shaping up to be a battle between the old versus new guard.

Party elections are set for Tuesday morning and will test how closely GOP members — angry over Republicans’ deep defeats and eager to chart a different course — tie their existing leadership team to the thrashing.

The ballot appears to be largely set for the House’s top three GOP positions after Speaker Mike Johnson said he would not run for top Republican again. After sending letters to colleagues yesterday, candidates will make their pitches to the rest of the conference before members vote in a secret tally. Friday is the deadline to declare candidacy.

Several members told Mia the race fallout could get ugly between incumbents and challengers. Here’s how the contests are shaking out:

— MINORITY LEADER: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise has thrown his hat in the ring against Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan to lead Republicans over the next two years, and the battle is expected to be bitter.

It’s a repeat of a faceoff between the two men in 2023. And Scalise, while seen as the more “steady hand” as one Republican put it, is also the most tied to Johnson.

“We got our asses kicked,” the member said. “And are they going to blame Scalise for that or the president? And are Republicans going to be happy if there are no scalps on the wall? Johnson already did, but does his first mate have to walk the plank too?”

— WHIP: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, as expected, will try to keep his role, and Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger challenged him yesterday. It’s not a surprising move: many knew Pfluger was angling for a leadership perch.

Several House Republicans say Emmer has broad conference support. But Pfluger could try to argue that GOP leadership should have pushed for more in another party-line bill this year.

— CONFERENCE CHAIR: GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain got a surprise challenge Wednesday night from Rep. Erin Houchin for the No. 3 job, focused on messaging.

McClain released a list of 35 members supporting her and her experience yesterday. Houchin’s name, meanwhile, was floated by several Republicans as a potential rising star.

The wild card in the elections? President Donald Trump, whose endorsement could easily sway a race. As of Wednesday, however, Trump said he wouldn’t choose sides in the minority leader fight.

What else we’re watching: 

— HOUSE DEM FACTIONS LOOK TO DISARM: After securing a huge majority, House Democrats’ warring factions say they are preparing to collaborate. This time last week, the progressive and moderate wings of the House Democratic Caucus were gearing up to battle for influence in what they thought might be a slim governing majority. But with some estimating the party will win as many as 260 seats, the prospect of having a 30-vote-minimum margin to pass legislation means no one group will come to the table with an obvious edge that would handcuff the likely incoming speaker, Hakeem Jeffries.

— GOP TRIES TO SALVAGE LAME DUCK: Republicans had a long list of priorities to wrap up in the lame-duck session. But Democrats may not be in the mood to compromise after their midterm election victories. Republicans will have to prioritize what they want to accomplish in their waning days of congressional control once Congress returns next week. Must-pass legislation both parties want to finish includes funding the government to avoid a pre-holiday shutdown and passing the annual defense authorization bill. Also in flux: whether Democrats will vote to enact a permitting deal reached before the election.

Riley Rogerson and Katherine Tully-McManus contributed to this report.

item.title: Democrats prepare for something new in the House: Teamwork
item.description: After securing a huge majority, House Democrats’ warring factions say they are preparing to collaborate.

media:content.media:title: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) arrives for a press conference with Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.) and other members of House Democratic leadership at 55 M St. SE in Washington, D.C. on Nov. 4, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
This time last week, the progressive and moderate wings of the House Democratic Caucus were gearing up to battle for influence in what they thought might be a slim governing majority. After surpassing expectations to win as many as 260 seats Tuesday night, members are showing signs of detente.

The results of the blowout midterm elections mean that House Democrats’ major ideological contingents will all swell in the next Congress. The centrist New Democrat Coalition is projecting at least 140 members, with the even more moderate Blue Dog Coalition grow to more than 20. The Congressional Progressive Caucus, meanwhile, is expected to have more than 100 members, six of whom identify as democratic socialists.

The prospect of having a 30-vote-minimum margin to pass legislation means no one group will come to the table with an obvious edge that would handcuff the likely incoming speaker, Hakeem Jeffries. If Democrats’ midterm gains had not been so pronounced, members might have more easily weaponized the narrow margins for their own political gains — by withholding their support for party-line bills, for instance, or opposing key procedural votes.

“There's been so much attention throughout the course of this campaign, because of some really tough primaries that happened very early on in the primary season, about intraparty squabbles among Democrats,” Rep. Greg Stanton of Arizona, who runs the centrist New Democrat Coalition’s campaign arm, told reporters Wednesday.

“But what happened last night was a political earthquake,” he continued, “where the American people demanded that checks and balances be restored to government.”

That’s not to say that Democrats won’t disagree next year. The caucus won’t unite overnight on whether to advance Medicare for All or end aid to Israel, and the party infighting over emotionally fraught issues could get ugly. Both moderate and progressive members insisted in interviews and media calls Wednesday that their proposals are best suited to satisfy voter demands to lower costs and tackle corruption.

“I've always said that being a progressive just means you're the first to the best and most just idea, and then everyone else runs to catch up with you,” said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, adding that it will be “the CPC [that] will continue to be a leading force in driving, accomplishing these ideas across the finish line.”

“Many of the policies [democratic socialists have] been championing just won’t hunt with the average Blue Dog and the district they represent,” said moderate Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, who added there are “plenty of policy areas where we can find common ground.”

Buoyed by their massive new mandate, however, Democrats were starting to talk about a deliberative, consensus-building blueprint for governing that would not involve hard-line tactics like those deployed by House Republicans over the last two years. Thanks to the GOP’s razor-thin majority, just a few members had the power to wrestle control of the floor from leadership and derail legislative business for days.

Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a member of the New Dems, said there will be a broad imperative to accommodate Democrats’ “big tent” and give some deference to the members who helped build the new House majority in swing districts.

He added, "It's a leadership challenge for all of us to make room for those folks to find those commonalities and overlap to develop relationships.”

Jeffries was leaning into consensus proposals at a news conference Wednesday morning. When asked about advancing policies like Medicare for All, he talked about legislation that the entire party backs — reversing Republican-led Medicaid cuts and extending enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits.

“We'll have a family conversation when we get back, and certainly in the new Congress, about what's the best way to do that beyond what we know we need to do immediately,” Jeffries said about health care.

The House will gavel back into session next week, and sitting Democrats will gather with incoming freshmen for orientation — an early opportunity for members from disparate ideological factions to find common ground. It could help that the next two years will be more about building a platform for 2028 rather than trying to actually pass laws given the likelihood of a presidential veto.

Rep. Delia Ramirez of Illinois last month said she and her progressive colleagues were coming up with a list of “non-negotiables” for a House Democratic majority platform. In an interview Wednesday she said the party’s vote cushion would work to progressives’ advantage: “There's no excuse that we can't, in fact, pass Medicare for All because we can't put these three frontliners on the line.”

Rep. Greg Meeks of New York, the likely incoming chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and an ally of leadership, said in an interview Tuesday night as the polls were closing that he was optimistic Democrats would “compromise among ourselves for the benefit of the American people.”

“I think that's what we're going to do,” he said. “That's why I think that the candidates that turned red seats into blue seats, that's why they ran.”

item.title: Thune's chat with Trump
item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune spoke Wednesday with President Donald Trump after the party's sweeping losses Tuesday, according to a person granted anonymity to disclose the private discussion.

The conversation comes amid speculation in and out of the Capitol about whether Trump would publicly stand by Thune if the GOP lost its Senate majority. But so far Trump has stayed silent on Thune while telling reporters Wednesday he would stay out of the brewing House GOP leadership race.

Thune has long said he intends to run for another term as leader, and GOP senators believe he'll keep the job. A spokesperson reiterated Wednesday he will run for leader in Tuesday's closed-door election.

item.title: Emmer's whip pitch
item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer launched his run for the minority whip job Wednesday in a letter to fellow Republican lawmakers, telling them, “There is no sugarcoating the failure we just experienced.”

“We lost, and I take that loss personally, both as a competitor and a member of this team,” the Minnesotan wrote about Tuesday’s results, adding, “We are down, but we are not out.”

Emmer, the No. 3 GOP leader since 2022, would rise to the No. 2 position if successful. He is expected to face Rep. August Pfluger, chair of the influential Republican Policy Committee.

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries announces run for speaker, promising ‘dramatic change’
item.description: With a huge majority and no expected competition, he is likely to cruise to the speakership.

media:content.media:title: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) departs a press conference in Washington, on Nov. 4, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is running for speaker, he announced in a letter to colleagues Wednesday.

Democrats have long considered the New Yorker — who has served two terms as minority leader — the heir apparent to longtime leader Nancy Pelosi. If he wins the Jan. 3 floor vote, he would become the House’s first Black speaker.

“Against all odds, House Democrats were consistently successful in the minority,” Jeffries wrote in the letter. “We must now deliver the dramatic change the American people are demanding in the majority.”

Jeffries is well-positioned to lead House Democrats next term. Although an incoming crop of hard-left members has not committed to backing him for speaker, no alternative candidate has emerged, and the size of the Democratic majority appears likely to make a small group of holdouts irrelevant.

In his role leading the caucus, Jeffries has built a reputation as a measured, deliberative leader with strong allies in the Congressional Black Caucus and centrist New Democrat Coalition. His left flank has signaled that they will push him on key priorities like Medicare for All and Israel aid.

In the letter, Jeffries touted his efforts to oppose President Donald Trump’s policies and personnel and working to overcome the “Republican gerrymandering scheme” by helping to organize counterefforts in California and elsewhere.

Jeffries emphasized on the campaign trail that he wants to tackle cost-lowering policies that could win broad support in the caucus. In particular, he previewed early votes on ending the Trump administration’s tariffs, clawing back Republican-led Medicaid cuts and restoring expired Affordable Care Act tax credits.

He also vowed an aggressive oversight agenda that includes probes into Trump, his family, his administration and his corporate allies.

Chris Marquette contributed to this report.

item.title: DeLauro makes official bid to return to the top job on the House Appropriations Committee
item.description: In a pitch to Democratic colleagues, she touted her revival of earmarks and relentless pushback against the Trump administration

media:content.media:title: House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) confers with Rep. John Carter (R-Texas) after a hearing on Capitol Hill on May 12, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Katherine Tully-McManus and Jennifer Scholtes
item.dc:contributor: By Katherine Tully-McManus and Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut officially launched her bid to chair the House Appropriations Committee for the second time after Democrats clinched control of the House in Tuesday's midterm election.

DeLauro, who is 83 and has served in the House since 1991, is currently the panel's top Democrat and is expected to easily win the gavel for the 120th Congress.

“If re-elected as chair, I intend to use the gavel to further increase domestic investments in health care, education, job training, housing, transportation, energy, protecting the environment, economic development, consumer protection, and cutting-edge research all of which will help bring down costs and ease the strain on working families,” she wrote in a letter Wednesday to Democratic colleagues.

She touted her record as chair in 2021 and 2022, when she restored lawmakers' ability to secure earmarks, or "Community Project Funding," for projects in their districts and states. DeLauro also announced plans this time around to “claw back billions of dollars Republicans unilaterally provided to Border Patrol, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Pentagon through budget reconciliation in an end run outside of the Appropriations Committee."

Democrats will be running up against a Republican White House the next two years, where President Donald Trump could threaten to veto legislation he doesn't like. They also won't have a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate to advance legislation along party lines.

But DeLauro and her counterpart, top Senate Appropriations Democrat Patty Murray of Washington, have been leading the charge against the Trump administration’s attempts to exert greater executive branch control over federal spending decisions, including its withholding of funding previously approved by Congress, including through “pocket rescissions."

DeLauro on Wednesday pledged to hold the Trump administration to account for these sorts of funding freezes, transfers and diversions that Democrats allege broke the law.

“Mark my words: if re-elected as chair, wherever and whenever this administration has violated the law with regard to the use of federal funds, I will hold them accountable,” DeLauro wrote.

item.title: Latest called races extend Democrats’ deluge
item.description: Democrats have secured another cache of wins, including key flips in Michigan.

media:content.media:title: Michigan Democratic House candidate William Lawrence speaks at an election night event Nov. 4, 2026, in Lansing, Michigan.

item.dc:creator: By Casey He
item.content:encoded:
Winners have been called in several remaining races as the historic blue wave continues to help Democrats make gains across the country.

In Michigan’s 4th District, Democratic state Sen. Sean McCann succeeded in his challenge to Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga. The eight-term GOP representative fought an uphill battle in the Kalamazoo-based district that he won by 12 points in 2024.

Democrat Christina Hines beat out Republican Michael Bouchard in a seat occupied by Rep. John James, the GOP gubernatorial candidate. James won the 10th District, which covers Detroit’s northern suburbs, by 6 points in 2024.

Democrat William Lawrence defeated freshman Republican Rep. Tom Barrett in Michigan’s 7th District. Barrett won the Lansing-based district, formerly held by Sen. Elissa Slotkin, by 4 points in 2024.

Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a moderate Democrat known for breaking with the party on key issues, won reelection for a third term in Washington’s 3rd District. She fended off a challenge from Republican state Senate Minority Leader John Braun in a traditionally right-leaning district that went for President Donald Trump by 3 points in 2024.

In Texas’ 9th District, Democrat Leticia Gutierrez won over Republican Alex Mealer to succeed Democratic Rep. Al Green, who unsuccessfully ran for a different seat after state Republicans redrew maps last year in hopes of bolstering Republicans’ advantage there. The Houston-area district was a target of the redistricting plan, and the result was another blow to the state GOP as Democrats swept statewide races in the Lone Star State.

In California’s 13th District, Democrat Adam Gray, who won his seat by 187 votes in 2024, handily secured reelection over Republican Kevin Lincoln. The district shifted to be friendlier to Democrats following California Democrats’ redistricting push last year.

In California’s 22nd District, progressive Democrat Randy Villegas, who was among Sen. Bernie Sanders’ handful of House endorsements, ousted Republican Rep. David Valadao in another newly drawn district where 2 out of 3 voters are Hispanic.

In California’s 34th District, democratic socialist Angela Gonzales‑Torres beat her incumbent opponent, fellow Democrat Jimmy Gomez. Gomez is facing a House Ethics Committee investigation after a former congressional staffer accused him of sexual misconduct. He has denied any wrongdoing.

New York Democratic Reps. Tom Suozzi and Laura Gillen both fended off their Republican challengers in the state’s 3rd and 4th districts, respectively.

item.title: Trump staying out of House GOP drama
item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday he's staying out of the race for House minority leader.

Sitting Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan have both announced runs following Speaker Mike Johnson's decision to step aside, and both are close allies of Trump. The president told reporters he's not choosing sides.

"We'll stay out of it," he said, then briefly mentioning Jordan. "But the speaker was fantastic. The people under him were fantastic. All good people. I guess right now you have two candidates, right?"

item.title: Lisa McClain launches repeat bid for House GOP conference chair
item.description: She promised to “get back in the fight” after Tuesday’s sweeping losses.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) said that the work being done by Republicans this week on reconciliation is "not gonna be perfect."

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan asked GOP colleagues Wednesday to reelect her as Republican conference chair, the No. 3 House leadership position, promising to “get back in the fight” after Tuesday’s sweeping losses.

In a letter obtained first by POLITICO, she said Republicans must “drive the national conversation” and “make sure the American people know what's at stake” as Democrats take control of the House.

“We must also make sure every member has the tools and platforms to aggressively take the fight to the Democrats,” she wrote. “I know our members, understand the challenges facing their districts, and have built relationships and a communications operation ready to serve you immediately.”

McClain has held the conference chair position, which is traditionally focused on party messaging and internal member organizing, for the past two years. With Speaker Mike Johnson stepping aside as Republicans move into the minority, staying as chair would mean taking a step up the party leadership ladder.

“The Chair’s job is not to build a personal brand. It’s to elevate yours,” she said in the letter. “I represent a deep-red district in a purple state and understand that what works in one district may not work in another. I’ll make sure you have the resources, messages, and platforms to reach your constituents and bring your voice to a national audience.”

No other candidate has formally emerged but some Republicans want Rep. Kat Cammack of Florida to challenge McClain. The two ran against each other for the position in 2024, with McClain more than doubling Cammack’s support.

Republicans have until noon Friday to declare their candidacy. Leadership elections are scheduled to begin Tuesday after Congress returns to Washington.

McClain raised over $8.5 million this cycle, with $3.5 million given to other House Republicans.

item.title: NRCC Chair Richard Hudson concedes his race for reelection in North Carolina

media:content.media:title: National Republican Congressional Committee Chair U.S. Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) speaks on stage on the second day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 10, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Meredith Lee Hill and Andrew Howard
item.dc:contributor: By Meredith Lee Hill and Andrew Howard
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), the chair of the GOP’s House campaign arm, conceded his race for reelection, he confirmed in a statement shortly after POLITICO reported the decision.

The AP has not yet called the race. But the decision is a stark sign of just how far the country shifted left: The person responsible for getting House Republicans elected this cycle is accepting defeat in a district President Donald Trump carried by almost 16 points just two years ago.

He called Democrat Richard Ojeda to concede, Hudson said in the statement, which thanked his staff, constituents and family.

“Last night, the voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice, and I respect it,” Hudson wrote. “God is sovereign over my life, and He has a plan for all of us.”

“America is the greatest country, and I believe more than ever in the principles that make us great,” Hudson continued. “Whatever the future holds, I will keep fighting for those principles and for the people who believe in commonsense, conservative policies that will save our country and make the lives of the American people better.”

This would be the first time ever a chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee has lost in a general election. In 1992, the NRCC chair lost in a primary. North Carolina Republicans felt the pressure leading up to Election Day, with worries about a massive win by Roy Cooper in the Senate race likely endangering a slew of once safely red House seats like Hudson’s and others.

Ojeda, a veteran who lost a Senate race in West Virginia in 2020, was drastically outspent by Hudson. But in a sign that Democrats thought they could flip the seat, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee threw $130,000 behind Ojeda last week.
